challenges.name: job-state-machine-quiz
challenges.title: Who may finish this job?
challenges.description: Two late results from CodeDev workers: a stalled grading worker writing while the job runs elsewhere, and an export worker finishing a job an admin cancelled.

questions.question:
The fix proposed in code review for the grading worker:

UPDATE submissions SET status = $2, score = $3
WHERE id = $1 AND status = 'running';

(the worker sets status = 'running' when it picks up the job). Job log of another submission after the fix:

10:03:00.351  grade:s_90120  stalled, lock expired, moved back to wait   (w-3 paused)
10:03:00.902  grade:s_90120  active worker=w-7, sets status='running'
10:03:01.410  w-3 resumes, its sandbox run ended: failed (wall time exceeded)
10:03:01.415  w-3  UPDATE ... status='failed' WHERE id='s_90120' AND status='running'
10:03:04.118  w-7  sandbox result: passed, runs the same UPDATE with 'passed'

Statement: "With this WHERE clause, w-3's late 'failed' at 10:03:01.415 updates zero rows, so the submission ends as passed."
questions.explanation: False. At 10:03:01.415 the status is 'running' again, because w-7 set it when it picked up the job at 10:03:00.902. The condition status = 'running' is true, so w-3's stale 'failed' is written (rowCount 1). Then w-7's 'passed' at 10:03:04.118 finds status = 'failed' and updates zero rows: the submission ends as failed, the opposite of what the review intended. A state check rejects writes after a job has ended, but it cannot tell two attempts of the same running job apart. The update needs the owner as well, for example AND worker_id = $4 with an id unique per attempt (an attempt number or lock token), so only w-7 can finish attempt 2. The misconception is that "running" identifies one execution; it only identifies a state that several executions can pass through.

True. The update only matches a row that is still running and still owned by w-2. Zero rows means one of those changed since w-2 claimed it: here the admin's cancel at 14:20:12 moved it to cancelled (a lease timeout and a new owner would also give zero rows). Because the email is sent only when won is true, the side effect follows the transition instead of the work, so no link for a cancelled export goes out. Note what the fix does not do: w-2 still spent twenty minutes uploading 2.1 GB, because cancelling a transition does not stop a running worker; checking ownership in the heartbeat or between steps lets it stop early. The misconception is that the email belongs to the upload; it belongs to the successful transition.

challenges.name: job-state-machine
challenges.title: A job state machine that rejects what cannot happen
challenges.description: Every CodeDev background job (grade a submission, send a certificate email, recompute the leaderboard, generate a course export) has a state that only changes through events. Write applyEvent(jobs, event, maxAttempts): apply ONE event to the jobs map; if it is accepted, update the job and return null; if it is rejected, change nothing and return the reason. States: queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled, retrying. Checks, in this order (the first failing check gives the reason): 1. event.type is not one of enqueue, start, heartbeat, succeed, fail, timeout, cancel, retry-scheduled -> "unknown event type". 2. a fail event whose failure is not "retryable" or "permanent" -> "invalid failure kind". 3. enqueue of an existing job id -> "job already exists" (otherwise create the job: queued, attempts 0, workerId null, lastFailure null). 4. any other event for a job id that does not exist -> "unknown job". 5. the event is not allowed in the job's state -> "<type> not allowed when <state>" (for example "succeed not allowed when queued"); allowed: start from queued or retrying; heartbeat, succeed, fail and timeout from running; cancel from queued, running or retrying; retry-scheduled from failed. 6. heartbeat, succeed or fail from a workerId that is not the job's workerId -> "stale worker <workerId> (owner <job.workerId>)". 7. retry-scheduled when the last failure was permanent -> "permanent failure"; retry-scheduled when attempts >= maxAttempts -> "max attempts reached". Effects: start -> running, attempts + 1, workerId = event.workerId, lastFailure null; heartbeat -> no change; succeed -> succeeded, workerId null; fail -> failed, lastFailure = event.failure, workerId null; timeout -> failed, lastFailure "retryable", workerId null; cancel -> cancelled, workerId null; retry-scheduled -> retrying. Input (JSON on stdin): { maxAttempts, events }. The runner prints one line per rejected event ("rejected #<1-based position> <type> <jobId>: <reason>"), then every job in the order it was enqueued ("<id> <state> attempts=<n>"). Up to about 1,100 events.
hints: For each event, which two facts about the job decide whether it may happen: the state it is in, and who is sending the event? Which events have a sender that must match, and which come from the system or an admin?

Look at the order of the checks in the description: validation of the event itself first, then whether the job exists, then the state, then the owner, then the retry rules. A table from event type to the list of states it is allowed in replaces most of the if statements. And check that a rejected event returns before any field of the job is changed.

A similar trace with maxAttempts 2 on an export job: enqueue x_1 -> queued. start(w1) -> running, attempts 1, owner w1. timeout -> failed, last failure retryable, owner cleared. heartbeat(w1) -> rejected: heartbeat is only allowed when running, and the job is failed. retry-scheduled -> retrying (attempts 1 < 2). start(w2) -> running, attempts 2, owner w2. fail(w1, retryable) -> rejected as a stale worker, because w1 is not the owner. fail(w2, retryable) -> failed. retry-scheduled -> rejected: attempts 2 is not below 2.
